facts.statement: The holotype specimen of Ichthyovenator is estimated to have been 8.5 to 10.5 meters long and weighed 2.4 tons.

facts.statement: In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated Ichthyovenator was approximately 8.5 meters long and weighed 2 tons.
facts.quote: In 2016, Gregory S. Paul estimated Ichthyovenator to have been approximately 8.5 m long and to have weighed 2 t.

facts.statement: Ichthyovenator had conical, straight teeth that lacked serrations.
facts.quote: Ichthyovenators teeth were conical, straight, and bore no serrations.

facts.statement: Ichthyovenator possessed a sail on its back and hips formed by elongated neural spines, a trait shared with many other spinosaurids.
facts.quote: Like many other spinosaurids, Ichthyovenator had a sail on its back and hips that was formed by the elongated neural spines of its vertebrae.

facts.statement: Uniquely among known spinosaurids, Ichthyovenator's sail was divided into two sections over the hips and featured a wave-like curvature.
facts.quote: Uniquely among known members of the family, Ichthyovenators sail was divided in two over the hips and had a sinusoid (wave-like) curvature.

facts.statement: The neural spine of the twelfth dorsal vertebra in Ichthyovenator was 54.6 cm high and had a trapezoidal shape, differing from the roughly rectangular spines of other known spinosaurids.
facts.quote: The 54.6 cm high spine of the twelfth dorsal vertebra widened towards the top, giving it a trapezoidal shape—similar to the condition seen in a neural spine from Vallibonavenatrix—whereas the spines of other known spinosaurids were roughly rectangular.

facts.statement: Ichthyovenator had a blade-like ilium measuring 92 cm long, which was proportionally longer relative to its 65 cm pubic bone than in any other known large theropod.
facts.quote: The 92 cm long ilium of the pelvis was blade-like, and longer in proportion to the 65 cm long pubic bone than that of any other known large theropod.

facts.statement: The ischium of Ichthyovenator was 49.6 cm long, representing a shorter proportion relative to the pubis than in any other known tetanuran theropod.
facts.quote: The ischium was 49.6 cm long, making it shorter in relation to the pubis than in all other known tetanuran theropods.

facts.statement: The shaft of Ichthyovenator's ischium was flattened sideways and lacked an expanded ischiadic apron, a condition also found in Monolophosaurus and Sinraptor.
facts.quote: The shaft of the ischium was flattened sideways, and had an unexpanded ischiadic apron, as in Monolophosaurus and Sinraptor.

facts.statement: In 2012, researchers identified the thirteenth dorsal neural spine as being 410% the length of the centrum.
facts.quote: In 2012, Ichthyovenator describers established the unique derived traits of the genus: its dorsal and sacral sinusoidal sail; the thirteenth dorsal neural spine being 410% the length of the centrum, and its distinct, finger-shaped process on its front upper corner

facts.statement: In 2012, Allain and colleagues classified Ichthyovenator as a basal member of the subfamily Baryonychinae within Spinosauridae.
facts.quote: In 2012, Allain and colleagues assigned Ichthyovenator to the Spinosauridae; more precisely to the subfamily Baryonychinae in a basal position as the sister taxon of a clade formed by Baryonyx and Suchomimus.

facts.statement: In 2014, Allain reclassified Ichthyovenator into the subfamily Spinosaurinae based on tooth morphology and vertebral similarities.
facts.quote: In Allain's 2014 abstract, he found Ichthyovenator instead as belonging to the Spinosaurinae, due to the lack of serrations on its teeth and the similarities of its vertebrae to those of Sigilmassasaurus.

facts.statement: A 2015 study suggested that Ichthyovenator possesses traits of both subfamilies, implying the distinction between Baryonychinae and Spinosaurinae may be unclear.
facts.quote: In a 2015 phylogenetic analysis by Evers and colleagues, they suggested the apparent presence of both baryonychine and spinosaurine characteristics in Ichthyovenator means the distinction between the two subfamilies may not be as clear as previously thought.

facts.statement: In 2017, Mickey Mortimer hypothesized that Ichthyovenator was a sail-backed carcharodontosaurid related to Concavenator instead of a spinosaurid.
facts.quote: In 2017, American palaeontologist Mickey Mortimer informally hypothesized Ichthyovenator may have been a sail-backed carcharodontosaurid dinosaur closely related to Concavenator, rather than a spinosaurid.

facts.statement: A 2017 analysis proposed that Baryonychinae might be a paraphyletic group, with species like Irritator and Angaturama acting as transitional forms.
facts.quote: A 2017 analysis by Sales and Schultz questioned Baryonychinae's validity, citing the morphology of Brazilian spinosaurids Irritator and Angaturama, and suggesting they may have been transitionary forms between the earlier baryonychines and the later spinosaurines.

facts.statement: In 2019, Thomas Arden and colleagues supported the classification of Ichthyovenator as a basal spinosaurine due to its tall dorsal sail.
facts.quote: Ichthyovenators spinosaurine classification was supported by Thomas Arden and colleagues in 2019, who resolved it as a basal member of the group due to its tall dorsal sail.

facts.statement: Although no skull remains of Ichthyovenator exist, related spinosaurids possessed elongated, narrow snouts similar to modern crocodilians.
facts.quote: Though no skull remains have been found for Ichthyovenator, all known spinosaurids had elongated, low, narrow snouts that allowed them to reach far for food and to quickly close their jaws in a manner similar to modern crocodilians.

facts.statement: The morphology of Ichthyovenator's jaws and teeth has led many paleontologists to believe spinosaurids were primarily piscivorous.
facts.quote: This type of jaw and tooth morphology, which is also observed in today's gharials and other fish-eating predators, has led many palaeontologists to believe spinosaurids were largely piscivorous (as implied by Ichthyovenators name).

facts.statement: Evidence such as iguanodontid bones in a Baryonyx specimen suggests some spinosaurids may have had a more generalist diet including larger prey.
facts.quote: A more generalist diet has also been proposed for spinosaurs, based on fossils such as the bones of a juvenile iguanodontid that was also found in the same Baryonyx specimen, an "Irritator" tooth embedded in the vertebrae of a pterosaur, and tooth crowns from Siamosaurus that were found in association with sauropod dinosaur bones.

facts.statement: Although no limb bones of Ichthyovenator are known, related spinosaurids had enlarged thumb claws used for hunting and processing prey.
facts.quote: Though no limb bones are known from Ichthyovenator, all known spinosaurids had well-built arms with enlarged thumb claws, which they likely used to hunt and process prey.

facts.statement: In 2013, Darren Naish favored sexual selection over species recognition for Ichthyovenator's sail, noting it evolved independently without close relatives.
facts.quote: In a 2013 blog post, Darren Naish considered the latter function unlikely, favouring the hypothesis of sexual selection for Ichthyovenators sail because it appears to have evolved on its own, without very close relatives.

facts.statement: Spinosaurids like Ichthyovenator likely had semiaquatic lifestyles, inferred from limb bone density and oxygen isotope ratios in their teeth.
facts.quote: Spinosaurids appear to have had semiaquatic lifestyles, spending much of their time near or in water, which has been inferred by the high density of their limb bones that would have made them less buoyant, and the oxygen isotope ratios of their teeth being closer to those of remains from aquatic animals like turtles, crocodilians, and hippopotamuses than those of other, more terrestrial theropods.

facts.statement: In 2019, Arden and colleagues suggested Ichthyovenator's short pelvis and elongated tail spines indicate spinosaurids used their tails for underwater propulsion.
facts.quote: Arden and colleagues in 2019 suggested the shortness of Ichthyovenators pubis and ischium relative to its ilium, coupled with the elongation of the neural spines in the tails of early spinosaurines, are indications that spinosaurids may have progressively made more use of their tails to propel themselves underwater as they grew more adapted to an aquatic lifestyle.
